question: Member States were required to transpose the revised Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD) by 29 May 2026. In Polish public debate, including in Podhale, there are concerns that future energy efficiency requirements could lead to pressure to make changes to traditional wooden architecture (Zakopane-style log houses) that would put aesthetic and cultural heritage values at risk.

At the same time, the Commission indicates that the directive allows for exemptions for, among other things, historical buildings and that Member States are free to choose renovation measures that suit their national context. In connection with the above: 1.

How does the Commission interpret the scope of permitted exemptions/derogations for buildings that are protected due to their historical or architectural value – especially when an unacceptable change in appearance would be required to meet the standards?
Is the Commission planning to publish (or has it already published) guidelines for the practical reconciliation of the EPBD with heritage conservation in regions with specific building traditions?

When assessing the transposition of the EPBD, will the Commission consider national solutions that more broadly protect regional heritage (e.g. Podhale’s wooden buildings) compatible with the directive through exemptions or less stringent requirements?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.8.2026) For residential buildings, the recast Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD)1 does not require mandatory improvements to individual buildings but imposes an average improvement at national level. Member States have flexibility as regards which part of their building stock they focus on, while at the same time prioritising the worst-performing ones.

For non-residential buildings, Member States may exclude protected ones from the obligation to achieve minimum levels of energy performance. In doing so, Member States are responsible for defining the protected status according to national rules and the level of exemptions granted to such buildings.

In 2025, the Commission adopted a support package2 offering guidance to help EU countries implement and transpose the EPBD including on exemptions for protected buildings3. Many renovation measures can be applied without compromising architectural or historical merits thanks to technological innovations. Some EU-supported practical resources are available.

4 In assessing transposition, the Commission will verify compliance with the Directive, while considering the flexibility allowed to develop tailor-made solutions reflecting local building characteristics. The Commission supports efforts to protect the cultural heritage value of buildings.
